lessons.title: Meet the pump
lessons.fact: The heart is a muscular pump about the size of a fist. It sits in the middle of the chest between the lungs, behind the sternum, tilted to the left. At rest it beats about 60-100 times a minute, pushing blood through the blood vessels to deliver O2 and nutrients and carry away CO2 and wastes.
lessons.rick: A meat pump the size of your fist. Beats about 100,000 times a day and never takes a day off. Unlike Jerry.

lessons.title: Four chambers, two pumps
lessons.fact: The heart has 4 chambers. The two upper ones, the atria, RECEIVE blood. The two lower ones, the ventricles, PUMP it out. The right side sends O2-poor blood to the lungs; the left side sends O2-rich blood to the whole body, so the left ventricle has the thickest, strongest wall.
lessons.rick: Two pumps glued together, genius. Right side does lungs, left side does everything else. Even you can count to four.

lessons.title: Arteries, veins, capillaries
lessons.fact: Arteries carry blood AWAY from the heart; veins carry it back TOWARD the heart. Capillaries are microscopic vessels with walls one cell thick, where O2 and nutrients leave the blood and wastes enter it. The aorta is the biggest artery. Arteries usually carry O2-rich blood; the pulmonary arteries are the main exception.
lessons.rick: Arteries: Away. Both start with A. That's the whole trick, Morty-brain. I *burp* just saved you a semester.

lessons.title: What blood is made of
lessons.fact: An adult has about 5 liters of blood. About 55% is plasma: water carrying proteins, salts, nutrients and hormones. The rest is mostly cells: red blood cells carry O2 using hemoglobin, white blood cells fight infection, and platelets (tiny cell fragments) plug leaks and help blood clot.
lessons.rick: Five liters of red soup. Red cells deliver, white cells fight, platelets patch holes. Better run than the Citadel.

questions.q: How many chambers does the human heart have?
questions.explain: Four: two atria on top that receive blood and two ventricles below that pump it out. A muscular wall, the septum, keeps the right side's O2-poor blood separate from the left side's O2-rich blood.

questions.q: Which blood vessels carry blood AWAY from the heart?
questions.explain: Arteries carry blood away from the heart under high pressure, so they have thick, muscular, elastic walls. Veins bring blood back and have thinner walls and valves. It's about direction, not oxygen: the pulmonary arteries carry O2-poor blood.

questions.q: Where do O2 and nutrients actually pass from the blood into the tissues?
questions.explain: Capillary walls are only one cell thick, so O2, nutrients and wastes can diffuse across them. Arteries, veins and the aorta have walls far too thick for exchange; they are the delivery and return pipes.
questions.rick: Capillaries. The tiny pipes where the actual work happens. Like grad students.

questions.q: Which blood cells carry oxygen?
questions.explain: Red blood cells are packed with hemoglobin, an iron-containing protein that binds O2. White blood cells defend against infection, platelets help clotting, and plasma cells are immune cells that make antibodies.

questions.q: What is the main job of platelets?
questions.explain: Platelets are small cell fragments that stick to damaged vessel walls and to each other, forming a plug, and help the clotting process that seals the leak. Fighting infection is the job of white blood cells.
questions.rick: Platelets are the duct tape of your blood. Cheap, tiny, and holding your whole sorry life together.

questions.q: Where does the RIGHT ventricle pump blood?
questions.explain: The right ventricle pumps O2-poor blood through the pulmonary trunk to the lungs to pick up O2. The LEFT ventricle pumps blood to the rest of the body through the aorta. In a normal heart the two sides never mix.
questions.rick: Right side, lungs. Left side, everything else. It's a two-pump system, not a riddle.

questions.q: Which heart chamber has the thickest muscular wall?
questions.explain: The left ventricle must push blood through the entire body at high pressure, so its wall is roughly three times thicker than the right ventricle's, which only pumps to the nearby, low-pressure lungs. The atria have the thinnest walls.
questions.rick: The left ventricle. It does the heavy lifting, so it hits the gym. The atria are just the warm-up act.

questions.q: A normal resting heart rate for an adult is about:
questions.explain: Most adults rest at about 60-100 beats per minute. Below 60 is called bradycardia and above 100 tachycardia, although very fit athletes often rest in the 40s or 50s quite normally.

questions.q: Click the left ventricle.
questions.explain: The left ventricle is the big, thick-walled lower chamber that forms the heart's tip (apex). It pumps O2-rich blood into the aorta and out to the whole body. On a front view it is on the viewer's RIGHT, because the patient's left is your right.

questions.q: Click the chamber that receives O2-poor blood returning from the body.

questions.q: Click the aorta, the body's largest artery.

questions.rick: The aorta. Biggest artery you've got. The garden hose of life, *burp* under serious pressure.

lessons.title: The route, step by step
lessons.fact: Body -> venae cavae -> right atrium -> tricuspid valve -> right ventricle -> pulmonary valve -> pulmonary trunk -> lungs (gain O2, lose CO2) -> pulmonary veins -> left atrium -> mitral valve -> left ventricle -> aortic valve -> aorta -> body. Pulmonary arteries carry O2-poor blood; pulmonary veins carry O2-rich blood.

lessons.title: Valves and heart sounds
lessons.fact: Four valves keep blood moving one way. The atrioventricular (AV) valves - tricuspid (right) and mitral, or bicuspid (left) - are tethered by chordae tendineae to papillary muscles. The semilunar valves - pulmonary and aortic - guard the exits. S1 'lub' = AV valves closing; S2 'dub' = semilunar valves closing.

lessons.title: The heart's wiring
lessons.fact: The SA node in the right atrium is the natural pacemaker. Its impulse spreads over both atria, is delayed at the AV node so the ventricles can fill, then runs down the bundle of His, bundle branches and Purkinje fibers. ECG: P wave = atrial depolarization, QRS = ventricular depolarization, T wave = ventricular repolarization.
lessons.rick: Self-wiring meat with a built-in *burp* metronome. Honestly? One of evolution's better hacks.

lessons.title: Output, red cells, blood types
lessons.fact: Cardiac output = heart rate x stroke volume: about 70/min x 70 mL, roughly 5 L/min at rest. Red cells come from red bone marrow (driven by EPO from the kidneys), have no nucleus and live about 120 days. ABO: plasma has antibodies against the A/B antigens your red cells lack, so type O has anti-A and anti-B; type AB has neither.

questions.q: Which valve lies between the LEFT atrium and the LEFT ventricle?
questions.explain: The mitral (bicuspid) valve has two cusps and sits between the left atrium and left ventricle. The tricuspid is its right-side twin. The aortic and pulmonary valves are semilunar valves at the ventricle exits.

questions.q: Which vessels carry O2-rich blood from the lungs to the heart?
questions.explain: The pulmonary veins (usually four) return freshly oxygenated blood from the lungs to the left atrium. They break the 'veins carry O2-poor blood' habit because vessels are named by direction - toward the heart - not by oxygen content.
questions.rick: Veins full of oxygen. Rules are for people who don't read the fine print.

questions.q: What is the heart's natural pacemaker?
questions.explain: The sinoatrial (SA) node fires spontaneously the fastest, about 60-100 times a minute, so it sets the pace. If it fails, the AV node can take over, but at a slower intrinsic rate of about 40-60 per minute.
questions.rick: SA node. The tiny drummer in your right atrium. Fire him and the whole band plays slower.

questions.q: On an ECG, the QRS complex represents:
choices: The delay in the AV node

questions.q: The first heart sound (S1, 'lub') is caused by:

Closing of the aortic and pulmonary valves
Opening of the mitral and tricuspid valves

questions.q: Heart rate is 70 beats/min and stroke volume is 70 mL. Cardiac output is about:
questions.explain: Cardiac output = heart rate x stroke volume = 70 x 70 mL = 4,900 mL/min, about 4.9 L/min - roughly your whole blood volume every minute at rest. During hard exercise it can rise to about 20-25 L/min.
questions.rick: Multiply two numbers. That's it. A calculator watch could replace you, Morty-brain.

questions.q: About how long does a red blood cell survive in the circulation?
questions.explain: With no nucleus, red cells can't repair themselves; after about 120 days they are removed, mainly by macrophages in the spleen, and their iron is recycled. EPO from the kidneys drives the bone marrow to replace them.
questions.rick: 120 days, then the spleen eats them. No nucleus, no repairs. Planned obsolescence, biology-style.

questions.q: A person with blood type O has which antibodies in their plasma?
questions.explain: Type O red cells carry neither A nor B antigen, and the plasma has antibodies against both. That's why O-negative red cells are the emergency 'universal donor' cells, while type O people can receive only type O red cells.
questions.rick: Type O: no antigens, all the antibodies. The paranoid bouncer of blood types. I respect it.

questions.q: Click the vein that returns blood from the head and arms to the heart.
questions.explain: The superior vena cava drains the head, neck, arms and upper chest into the top of the right atrium. Its partner, the inferior vena cava, brings blood up from the lower body.
questions.rick: Superior vena cava. 'Superior' because it's on top, not because it's better than you. Though it is.

questions.q: Click the vessel that carries blood from the right ventricle toward the lungs.
questions.explain: The pulmonary trunk leaves the right ventricle through the pulmonary valve and splits into the right and left pulmonary arteries. It is an artery carrying O2-poor blood: direction, not oxygen, defines an artery.

lessons.title: Cardiac action potentials
lessons.fact: Ventricular cells rest near -90 mV. Phase 0: fast Na+ influx. Phase 2 plateau: Ca2+ in via L-type channels balances K+ out. Phase 3: K+ efflux repolarizes. The long plateau means a long refractory period, so heart muscle can't tetanize. SA/AV node cells: phase 4 drifts up via the 'funny' Na+ current (If); their upstroke is Ca2+.

lessons.title: Stroke volume and Starling
lessons.fact: Stroke volume depends on preload (end-diastolic stretch), afterload (pressure the ventricle ejects against) and contractility (raised by sympathetic beta1 stimulation). Frank-Starling law: more stretch -> stronger beat, so output matches venous return. Ejection fraction = SV / EDV, normally about 55-70%.
lessons.rick: Stretch it more, it snaps back harder. Frank and Starling worked that out without a portal gun.

lessons.title: Listening posts and murmurs

Stenosis = can't open fully; regurgitation = can't close fully. Systolic murmurs: aortic stenosis, mitral regurgitation. Diastolic: mitral stenosis, aortic regurgitation.

lessons.title: Hemostasis: plug, then glue

Secondary: the coagulation cascade makes thrombin, which turns fibrinogen into fibrin to seal it. Factors II, VII, IX, X need vitamin K.

Decrease, because overstretched fibers can't contract

choices: Enlarged left ventricle compressing the esophagus

Enlarged right ventricle compressing the esophagus

lessons.title: Why you breathe
lessons.fact: Every cell needs O2 to make energy and produces CO2 as waste. Breathing brings fresh air in and gets rid of CO2. Air travels: nose or mouth -> pharynx (throat) -> larynx (voice box) -> trachea (windpipe) -> bronchi -> bronchioles -> alveoli. A resting adult breathes about 12-20 times a minute.

lessons.title: Two lungs, not twins
lessons.fact: The two lungs fill most of the chest, protected by the rib cage. They are spongy and light because they are mostly air. The right lung has 3 lobes; the left has only 2, leaving room for the heart. Each lung is wrapped in a thin, slippery membrane called the pleura.

lessons.title: The diaphragm does the work
lessons.fact: The diaphragm is a dome-shaped sheet of muscle under the lungs. When you breathe IN, it contracts and flattens, making the chest bigger so air rushes in. When you breathe OUT at rest, it simply relaxes and domes back up, pushing air out. Hiccups are sudden involuntary spasms of the diaphragm.
lessons.rick: A muscle trampoline under your lungs. Pull down, air in. Relax, air out. Even a Meeseeks gets it.

lessons.title: Alveoli: the swap meet
lessons.fact: The airways end in hundreds of millions of tiny air sacs called alveoli, each wrapped in capillaries. O2 diffuses from the air into the blood, and CO2 diffuses from the blood into the air to be breathed out. Spread flat, all that surface would cover roughly 70 square meters.

questions.q: Which gas do your lungs get rid of as a waste product?
questions.explain: Cells burn fuel with O2 and produce CO2, which the blood carries to the lungs to be breathed out. Nitrogen is about 78% of air but just goes in and out unused.

questions.q: Where in the lungs does gas exchange happen?
questions.explain: Alveoli are tiny air sacs with walls one cell thick, wrapped in capillaries, so O2 and CO2 can diffuse across. The trachea, bronchi and larynx are just pipes that carry air to them.

lessons.title: The airway tree

lessons.title: Conducting vs respiratory zone
lessons.fact: From the nose to the terminal bronchioles is the conducting zone: it warms, humidifies and filters air but exchanges no gas, so it is 'anatomic dead space' (about 150 mL). The respiratory zone - respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts and alveoli - is where gas exchange happens.

lessons.title: Pressure moves the air
lessons.fact: Inhaling: the diaphragm and external intercostals contract, chest volume rises, so alveolar pressure falls below atmospheric (Boyle's law) and air flows in. Quiet exhaling is passive elastic recoil. A quiet breath (tidal volume) is about 500 mL; about 1.2 L (residual volume) always stays in; total lung capacity is about 6 L.

lessons.title: Moving O2 and CO2

CO2 travels mostly (about 70%) as bicarbonate (HCO3-). Breathing is driven mainly by rising CO2, sensed by chemoreceptors in the medulla.

Alveolar pressure falls below atmospheric pressure

questions.q: How is most CO2 carried in the blood?

questions.q: How is most O2 carried in the blood?

questions.q: What is the volume of air left in the lungs after a maximal exhalation called?

questions.q: In a healthy person, the main chemical signal that drives breathing is:

questions.q: Click where O2 actually passes from the air into the blood.

lessons.title: Alveolar cells and surfactant
lessons.fact: Type I pneumocytes are thin, flat cells covering about 95% of the alveolar surface for gas exchange. Type II pneumocytes secrete surfactant (mainly dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine) and regenerate type I cells. Surfactant lowers surface tension so small alveoli don't collapse (Laplace: P = 2T/r) and raises lung compliance.

lessons.title: V/Q matching
lessons.fact: Overall ventilation/perfusion (V/Q) is about 0.8. Upright, both are greatest at the base, but perfusion rises more, so V/Q is highest at the apex (about 3) and lowest at the base (about 0.6). No blood flow (embolus): V/Q -> infinity, dead space. No airflow (blocked airway): V/Q = 0, shunt. Hypoxia constricts pulmonary vessels.

lessons.title: The O2-hemoglobin curve
lessons.fact: Hemoglobin binds O2 cooperatively, giving a sigmoid curve (P50 about 27 mmHg). A RIGHT shift means lower affinity and easier O2 unloading: more CO2, H+ (low pH), heat and 2,3-BPG, as in exercising muscle. LEFT shift: fetal hemoglobin (binds 2,3-BPG poorly), carbon monoxide, alkalosis, cold.

lessons.title: Airway anatomy

The right lung has 3 lobes; the left has 2, plus the cardiac notch and the lingula (part of its upper lobe). Bronchi have cartilage; bronchioles have none: smooth muscle dominates.

questions.q: In an upright person, where is the V/Q ratio highest?

lessons.title: Obstructive vs restrictive
lessons.fact: Obstructive (asthma, COPD): air gets in but can't get out - FEV1/FVC below 0.7, TLC normal or high (air trapping). parts.rick: Longer and skinnier, because the aorta is sitting on it. Rough neighborhood.

parts.name: Bronchioles
parts.desc: Small airways (under about 1 mm) beyond the bronchi, with no cartilage; smooth muscle dominates their walls. Terminal bronchioles end the conducting zone; respiratory bronchioles begin gas exchange.
parts.rick: Tiny tubes with no cartilage, all muscle and attitude. Squeeze too hard and you wheeze.

parts.name: Alveoli
parts.desc: Hundreds of millions of tiny air sacs wrapped in capillaries: the site of gas exchange. Lined by type I cells (thin exchange surface) and type II cells (surfactant).
parts.rick: Where the actual magic happens. Everything else is just pipes, Morty-brain.

parts.name: Right Lung
parts.desc: Larger lung with 3 lobes (upper, middle, lower) divided by the horizontal and oblique fissures. A bit shorter than the left because the liver pushes the diaphragm up on the right.
parts.rick: Three lobes. The overachiever. Basically the Rick of lungs.

parts.name: Left Lung
parts.desc: Smaller lung with 2 lobes (upper and lower) divided by the oblique fissure. Its upper lobe carries the cardiac notch and the lingula, making room for the heart.
parts.rick: Two lobes and a heart-shaped dent. Sentimental little organ.

parts.name: Cardiac Notch
parts.desc: Indentation in the front border of the left lung's upper lobe where the heart lies closest to the chest wall; the lingula sits just below it.
parts.rick: A dent made just for the heart. Romantic, if lungs had feelings. They don't. Neither do I.

parts.name: Diaphragm
parts.desc: Dome-shaped muscle separating the thorax from the abdomen; the main muscle of breathing. Contracts and flattens to inhale. Motor supply: the phrenic nerves (C3-C5).
parts.rick: The plunger under your lungs. C3-4-5 keeps it alive. *burp* Write that on your hand.
